```java
class GameOfLifeJava {
    public static String print(int[][] matrix) {
        StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();
        for (int[] row : matrix) {
            for (int cell : row)
                if (cell != 0) result.append('#');
                else result.append(' ');
            result.append('\n');
        }
        return result.toString();
    }
}
```

```java
class GameOfLifeJava {
    public static String print(int[][] matrix) {
        StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();
        for (int[] row : matrix) {
            for (int cell : row)
                if (cell != 0) result.append('#');
                else result.append(' ');
            result.append('\n');
        }
        return result.toString();
    }

    public static class Shape {
        private int[][] pattern;

        public Shape(int[][] pattern) {
            if (pattern.length < 1 || pattern[0].length < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
            this.pattern = pattern;
        }

        public int numRows() { return pattern.length; }
        public int numCols() { return pattern[0].length; }
        public int[][] getPattern() { return pattern; }
    }
}
```

```scala
  // Array(1, 0, 1)
  // should result in the string
```
```scala
  // " #\n#"
  def print(matrix: Array[Array[Int]]): String = {
    val result = new StringBuilder()
    for
      row <- matrix
      cell <- row
    do
      if cell != 0 then
        result.append("#")
      else
        result.append(" ")
      result.append("\n")
    result.toString()
  }
```

```scala
object GameOfLife:
```
class Game(val rows: Int, val cols: Int):
def step(): Unit =
  for i <- 0 until rows do
    for j <- 0 until cols do
      var alive = 0
      for ni <- -1 to 1 do
        for nj <- -1 to 1 do
          if i+ni>=0 && i+ni<rows
          && j+nj>=0 && j+nj<cols
          && (ni != 0 || nj != 0) then alive += board(i+ni)(j+nj)
      end for
      end for
      board(i)(j) match
        case 1 if alive < 2 => next(i)(j) = 0 // cell is lonely and dies
        case 1 if alive > 3 => next(i)(j) = 0 // cell is overpopulated and dies
        case 0 if alive == 3 => next(i)(j) = 1 // new cell born

```scala
object GameOfLife:
```
class Game(val rows: Int, val cols: Int):
def step(): Unit =
  for i <- 0 until rows do
    for j <- 0 until cols do
      var alive = 0
      for ni <- -1 to 1 do
        for nj <- -1 to 1 do
          if i+ni>=0 && i+ni<rows
          && j+nj>=0 && j+nj<cols
          && (ni != 0 || nj != 0) then alive += board(i+ni)(j+nj)
      end for
      end for
      board(i)(j) match
        case 1 if alive < 2 => next(i)(j) = 0 // cell is lonely and dies
        case 1 if alive > 3 => next(i)(j) = 0 // cell is overpopulated and dies
        case 0 if alive == 3 => next(i)(j) = 1 // new cell born

object GameOfLife:
class Game(val rows: Int, val cols: Int):
def step(): Unit =
  for i <- 0 until rows do
    for j <- 0 until cols do
      var alive = 0
      for ni <- -1 to 1 do
        for nj <- -1 to 1 do
          if i+ni>=0 && i+ni<rows
          && j+nj>=0 && j+nj<cols
          && (ni != 0 || nj != 0) then alive += board(i+ni)(j+nj)
      end for
      end for
      board(i)(j) match
        case 1 if alive < 2 => next(i)(j) = 0 // cell is lonely and dies
        case 1 if alive > 3 => next(i)(j) = 0 // cell is overpopulated and dies
        case 0 if alive == 3 => next(i)(j) = 1 // new cell born

Type: slide, code

Content:
Top: Unit Tests with ScalaTest

Left:
def factorial(n: Int): Int =
  var result = 1
  for i <- 1 to n do
    result *= i
  result

Right:
class FactorialTests
extends AnyFlatSpec with should.Matchers:
  "Factorial" should "compute 0! correctly" in {
    factorial(0) should be (1)
  }
  it should "compute 1! correctly" in {
    factorial(1) should be (1)
  }
  it should "compute 3! correctly" in {
    factorial(3) should be (6)
  }

Bottom:
• Matchers should be etc. express expected results
• ⚠ Can only test a finite number of examples

```scala
object GameOfLife:
  // Array(1, 0, 1)
  // should result in the string
  // " #\n#"
  def print(matrix: Array[Array[Int]]): String = {
    val result = new StringBuilder()
    for
      row <- matrix
      cell <- row
    do
      if cell != 0 then
        result.append("#")
      else
        result.append(" ")
      result.append("\n")
    result.toString()
  }
```

  require (n>=0)
  var result = 1
  for i <- 1 to n do
    result *= i
  result
} ensuring {
  (result: Int) =>
    result == factorialContract(n)
}

Top: Summary

Left:
Unit Tests
• Execute code with some inputs and test for expected outputs
  • + documents known and expected use and behavior
  • - finite number of tests
  • Best for: regression testing

Right:
Contracts
• Express input assumptions and output guarantees
  • + show correctness for all possible inputs and executions
  • - computational overhead, extra effort
  • Best for: correctness-critical applications

Title: Pattern Matching Example: Lists

Problem Statement:
In Scala, implement a method that takes a list of at least 3 numbers and returns it with the first 3 numbers sorted in ascending order.

Code:
def f(numbers: List[Int]): List[Int] = {
  require(numbers.length >= 3, "The list must contain at least 3 elements")
  val (firstThree, rest) = numbers.splitAt(3)
  firstThree.sorted ++ rest
} ensuring { (result: List[Int]) => ??? }

Bullet Point:
Contract for checking the first 3 elements

Left: Index access
ensuring {
  (result: List[Int]) =>
  val x1 = result(0)
  val x2 = result(1)
  val x3 = result(2)
  x1 <= x2 && x2 <= x3
}

Right: Projections
ensuring {
  (result: List[Int]) =>
  val x1 = result.head
  val x2 = result.tail.head
  val x3 = result.tail.tail.head
  x1 <= x2 && x2 <= x3
}

Content:
Title: Pattern Matching Example: Lists

Problem Statement:
In Scala, implement a method that takes a list of at least 3 numbers and returns it with the first 3 numbers sorted in ascending order.

Code Example:
```scala
def f(numbers: List[Int]): List[Int] = {
  require(numbers.length >= 3, "The list must contain at least 3 elements")
  val (firstThree, rest) = numbers.splitAt(3)
  firstThree.sorted ++ rest
} ensuring { (result: List[Int]) => ??? }
```

Contract for checking the first 3 elements:

Left: Index access
```scala
ensuring {
  (result: List[Int]) =>
  val x1 = result(0)
  val x2 = result(1)
  val x3 = result(2)
  x1 <= x2 && x2 <= x3
}
```

Middle: Projections
ensuring {
  (result: List[Int]) =>
  val x1 = result.head
  val x2 = result.tail.head
  val x3 = result.tail.tail.head
  x1 <= x2 && x2 <= x3
}

Right: Pattern matching
ensuring {
  (result: List[Int]) =>
  val x1 :: x2 :: x3 :: _ = result
  x1 <= x2 && x2 <= x3
}

Bottom Right: Alternative pattern matching
ensuring {
  case x1 :: x2 :: x3 :: _ =>
  x1 <= x2 && x2 <= x3
}

Code:
def f (xs: List[(Int,String)]) = xs match
  case Nil => "List is empty"
  case x :: Nil => s"List has one element: $x"
  case _ :: (x,_) :: _ => s"The second int is $x"
end f

Title: Pattern Matching Exercise: List Operations

Bullet 1: Implement simple list operations by pattern matching

Code blocks:
Left: isEmpty
def isEmpty (xs: List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => true
    case _ => false
end isEmpty

Middle: head
def head (xs: List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => throw NoSuchElementException()
    case y :: _ => y
end head

Right: tail
def tail (xs:List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => throw NoSuchElementException()
    case _ :: ys => ys
end tail

Bullet 2: Many list operations are builtin:
- List (1, 2, 3).head
- List (1, 2, 3).tail
- List (1, 2, 3).isEmpty

Content:
Title: Pattern Matching Exercise: List Operations

Bullet 1: Implement simple list operations by pattern matching

Code blocks:
Left: isEmpty
def isEmpty (xs: List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => true
    case _ => false
end isEmpty

Middle: head
def head (xs: List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => throw NoSuchElementException()
    case y :: _ => y
end head

Right: tail
def tail (xs:List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => throw NoSuchElementException()
    case _ :: ys => ys
end tail

Bullet 2: Many list operations are builtin:
- List (1, 2, 3).head
- List (1, 2, 3).tail
- List (1, 2, 3).isEmpty

  xs match
    case Nil => throw NoSuchElementException()
    case y :: _ => y
end head

def tail (xs:List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => throw NoSuchElementException()
    case _ :: ys => ys
end tail

Content:
Title: Pattern Matching Exercise: List Operations

Bullet 1: Implement simple list operations by pattern matching

Code blocks:
Left: isEmpty
def isEmpty (xs: List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => true
    case _ => false
end isEmpty

Middle: head
def head (xs: List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => throw NoSuchElementException()
    case y :: _ => y
end head

Right: tail
def tail (xs:List[Int]) =
  xs match
    case Nil => throw NoSuchElementException()
    case _ :: ys => ys
end tail

Bullet 2: Many list operations are builtin:
- List (1, 2, 3).head
- List (1, 2, 3).tail
- List (1, 2, 3).isEmpty

Content:
Title: Contracts

Text:
- Contracts are formal and verifiable interface specifications
  • Preconditions are expectations that must be met by a client
  • Postconditions are guarantees made by the component
  • Invariants are maintained (e.g., every loop iteration)

Content:
Title: Methods vs. Fields

Bullet Points:
- val field: val x = 1; strict, initialized once
- def non-parameterized method: def y = 2; non-strict, executed every time
- lazy val: memoized def, initialized on demand

Left: Scala
Code:
class C:
  val x = 1
  def y = 2
  lazy val z = x + y
end C

Right: Expressed in Java
Code:
public class C {
  public final int x = 1;
  public int y() { return 2; }
  private Integer z = null;
  public int z() {
    if (z == null) z = x + y();
    return z;
  }
}

2   case Nil => "List is empty"

5 end f

  - Nested patterns: patterns can include other patterns
  - Print first tuple of a singleton list, else print second int

Code:

2   case Nil => "List is empty"
3   case x :: Nil => s"List has one element: $x"
4   case _ :: (x,_) :: _ => s"The second int is $x"
5 end f

Top: Companion Objects

Left:
Java: static vs. non-static
• static components belong to a class
• All other belong to instance of class

Code:
1 class C {
2   private int f1 = 0;
3   private static int f2 = 0;
4
5   public int m1 () {
6     C.f2 = 3;
7     return f1;
8   }
9
10  public static int m2 (C other) {
11    other.f1 = 5;
12    return f2;
13  }
14 }

Right:
Scala: Companion object replaces static
• All data and methods belong to objects
• Companion related to other instances

Code (Matrix.scala):
```scala
class Matrix(val data: Array[Array[Int]]) {
  val rows: Int = data.length
  val cols: Int = data(0).length

  def +(other: Matrix): Matrix = {
    val result = Array.ofDim[Int](rows, cols)
    for (i <- 0 until rows; j <- 0 until cols) {
      result(i)(j) = this.data(i)(j) + other.data(i)(j)
    }
    new Matrix(result)
  }

  override def toString: String = data.map(_.mkString(", ")).mkString("\n")
}

object Matrix {

}
```

class Matrix(val data: Array[Array[Int]]):
  val rows: Int = data.length
  val cols: Int = data(0).length

  def +(other: Matrix): Matrix =
    val result = Array.ofDim[Int](rows, cols)
    for(i <- 0 until rows; j <- 0 until cols) do
      result(i)(j) = this.data(i)(j) + other.data(i)(j)
    end for
    new Matrix(result)
  end +

  def main(args: Array[String]): Unit = println("Hello, Matrix!")

class Matrix(val data: Array[Array[Int]]):
  val rows: Int = data.length
  val cols: Int = data(0).length

  def +(other: Matrix): Matrix =
    val result = Array.ofDim[Int](rows, cols)
    for(i <- 0 until rows; j <- 0 until cols) do
      result(i)(j) = this.data(i)(j) + other.data(i)(j)
    end for
    new Matrix(result)
end +

Text:
In computer programming, especially in functional programming and type theory, an algebraic data type (ADT) is a composite data type—a type formed by combining other types.

An algebraic data type is defined by two key constructions: a sum and a product. These are sometimes referred to as "OR" and "AND" types.

A sum type is a choice between possibilities. The value of a sum type can match one of several defined variants. For example, a type representing the state of a traffic light could be either Red, Amber, or Green. A shape type could be either a Circle (which stores a radius) or a Square (which stores a width). In formal terms, these variants are known as tagged unions or disjoint unions. Each variant has a name, called a constructor, which can also carry data. Enumerated types are a simple form of sum type where the constructors carry no data.

In computer programming, especially in functional programming and type theory, an algebraic data type (ADT) is a composite data type—a type formed by combining other types.

An algebraic data type is defined by two key constructions: a sum and a product. These are sometimes referred to as "OR" and "AND" types.

A sum type is a choice between possibilities. The value of a sum type can match one of several defined variants. For example, a type representing the state of a traffic light could be either Red, Amber, or Green. A shape type could be either a Circle (which stores a radius) or a Square (which stores a width). In formal terms, these variants are known as tagged unions or disjoint unions. Each variant has a name, called a constructor, which can also carry data. Enumerated types are a simple form of sum type where the constructors carry no data.

A product type combines types together. A value of a product type will contain a value for each of its component types. For

In computer programming, especially in functional programming and type theory, an algebraic data type (ADT) is a composite data type—a type formed by combining other types.

An algebraic data type is defined by two key constructions: a sum and a product. These are sometimes referred to as "OR" and "AND" types.

A sum type is a choice between possibilities. The value of a sum type can match one of several defined variants. For example, a type representing the state of a traffic light could be either Red, Amber, or Green. A shape type could be either a Circle (which stores a radius) or a Square (which stores a width). In formal terms, these variants are known as tagged unions or disjoint unions. Each variant has a name, called a constructor, which can also carry data. Enumerated types are a simple form of sum type where the constructors carry no data.

A product type combines types together. A value of a product type will contain a value for each of its component types. For

Formula: X ∪ Y = {z | z ∈ X ∨ z ∈ Y}

Bullet 2: Coproduct or disjoint union of sets
Formula: X ⊕ Y = X ⊕ Y = {(0, x) | x ∈ X} ∪ {(1, y) | y ∈ Y}

Title: Algebraic Data Types

Left:
- Product types
  - Combine multiple data elements into one unit
  - Tuples and classes
    Code:
    1 val product = (1, "hello", List(1, 2, 3))
- Algebraic Data Types (wikipedia) in PLs

Right:
- Sum types
  - Distinguish multiple alternatives
  - Union type Int | String
  - Discriminated union
    Code:
    1 class A
    2 class B extends A
    3 class C extends A

- Algebraic data type

  ```
  enum Tree[X]:
    case Leaf (data:X)
    case Node (l:Tree[X], f:(X,X)=>X, r:Tree[X])
  ```

Type: slide

Content:
Title: Algebraic Data Types

Left:
- Product types
  - Combine multiple data elements into one unit
  - Tuples and classes
    Code:
    1 val product = (1, "hello", List(1, 2, 3))
- Algebraic Data Types (wikipedia) in PLs

Right:
- Sum types
  - Distinguish multiple alternatives
  - Union type Int | String
  - Discriminated union
    Code:
    1 class A
    2 class B extends A
    3 class C extends A

============================================================
时间戳: 02:56:32 (10592.00s), OCR耗时: 0.00s, 平均耗时: 1.44s, InputTokens: 0, OutputTokens: 0
============================================================
Type: slide

Content:
Top: Summary

Left:
Unit Tests
• Execute code with some inputs and test for expected outputs
  • + documents known and expected use and behavior
  • - finite number of tests
  • Best for: regression testing

Right:
Contracts
• Express input assumptions and output guarantees
  • + show correctness for all possible inputs and executions
  • - computational overhead, extra effort
  • Best for: correctness-critical applications

  • Best for: regression testing

Right:
Contracts
• Express input assumptions and output guarantees
  • + show correctness for all possible inputs and executions
  • - computational overhead, extra effort
  • Best for: correctness-critical applications

============================================================
时间戳: 02:56:35 (10595.00s), OCR耗时: 1.75s, 平均耗时: 1.44s, InputTokens: 1397, OutputTokens: 147
============================================================
Type: slide, code

Content:
Top: Exercise: Binary Operations Tree

Left:
• Data stored at leaves
• Operations stored at internal nodes
• Internal nodes have left and right subtrees
• Algebraic data type
Code:
enum Tree[X]:
  case Leaf (data:X)
  case Node (l:Tree[X], f:(X,X)=>X, r:Tree[X])

Right:
• Fold tree into result by applying all the intermediate operations
• Recursive with pattern matching
Code:
def fold [X] (t: Tree[X]) : X = t match
  case Leaf(x) => x
  case Node(l, f, r) => f(fold(l), fold(r))

Content:
Title: Pure vs Side-Effecting Expressions

Bullet Points:
• A mathematical function takes arguments and gives results
• An expression is pure if that is all it does
• Pure expression does not modify store ξ
  Formula: (e₁,ξ₀)↓⟨v₁,ξ₁⟩ (e₂,ξ₁)↓⟨v₂,ξ₂⟩
           ----------------------------
           (e₁+e₂,ξ₀)↓⟨v₁+v₂,ξ₂⟩ (Add)
• Anything else is a side effect
  • Assignment to a variable
  • Change of control (goto)
  • I/O (console, network)
  • etc.

- Sum types
